words.definition: A state of success, wealth, and good fortune, often financial.
words.example: After years of drought, the good harvests finally brought prosperity to the village, and new shops opened everywhere.
words.mnemonic: Spock's blessing 'live long and PROSPER' is a wish for exactly this: long life and good times.

words.definition: Enjoying financial success and comfortable wealth.
words.example: The prosperous merchant arrived in a chauffeured car and tipped every waiter generously.
words.mnemonic: 'prosper' + '-ous' (full of) = full of prospering, so things are going great.

words.definition: To grow strong and do well, especially under favorable conditions.
words.example: Fish thrive in the clean, oxygen-rich water of the restored river.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'alive' and 'drive' — something full of life and drive is thriving.

words.definition: Money or profit, especially when viewed as morally tainted.
words.example: He abandoned his principles for the lucre of the arms trade, and old friends stopped speaking to him.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'Lucifer's' cash — the classic phrase 'filthy lucre' is money that feels sinful.

words.definition: Wealth treated as a god or object of greedy devotion.
words.example: The preacher warned the crowd not to serve mammon at the expense of their souls.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'MAMA-money' or 'MONEY-man' — the false god you bow to for cash.

words.definition: Property or an estate handed down from one's father or ancestors.
words.example: When his father died, the vineyards and the old stone house became his patrimony.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'pater' (father) + money = the wealth passed down from your father.

words.definition: Money or property received from someone after their death.
words.example: She used her grandmother's inheritance to pay off the mortgage and start a bakery.
words.mnemonic: Spot the 'HERIT' inside — the HEIR gets what lands in their hands.

words.definition: The total property and possessions a person owns, especially at death.
words.example: After the tycoon's death, lawyers spent months dividing his enormous estate among the heirs.
words.mnemonic: Think 'real ESTATE' scaled up: E-STATE, a whole state-sized holding of land and wealth.

words.definition: Having enough money to pay all one's debts.
words.example: Thanks to careful budgeting, the small charity remained solvent even during the recession.
words.mnemonic: If you can SOLVE your debts by paying them off, you are solvent.

words.definition: The ability to pay all one's debts when they come due.
words.example: The bank's solvency was questioned when it could no longer cover customer withdrawals.
words.mnemonic: 'SOLVE' + '-ency' = the state of being able to solve (pay off) what you owe.

words.definition: Rule of a society by its wealthiest people.
words.example: Critics argued the country had become a plutocracy, where only billionaires could influence the laws.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'Ploutos' (god of riches) + '-cracy' (rule) = government run by the rich.

words.definition: A very rich person who holds power because of that money.
words.example: The plutocrat funded three senators' campaigns and expected favorable votes in return.
words.mnemonic: 'Ploutos' (god of riches) + '-crat' (ruler) = one who rules thanks to riches.

words.definition: A rich, powerful leader in a particular industry or business.
words.example: The shipping magnate owned half the tankers in the harbor and a private island besides.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'MAGNET' — a business magnate pulls in money and power like a magnet.

words.definition: A wealthy, powerful person in business or industry.
words.example: The oil tycoon built a gleaming skyscraper and named it after himself.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'typhoon' — a business tycoon storms through an industry with money and might.

words.definition: A powerful, wealthy person who controls a large business or industry.
words.example: The film mogul owned three studios and could greenlight any movie with a single phone call.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'Mughal' — the fabulously rich Mughal emperors who ruled vast, wealthy empires.

words.definition: A person of conspicuous wealth or high status, often newly rich.
words.example: The colonel returned from the colonies a nabob, buying an estate and a fleet of carriages.
words.mnemonic: From 'nawab,' the wealthy provincial governors of Mughal India — rich rulers of provinces.

words.definition: Having a great deal of wealth.
words.example: Only the moneyed families could afford private boxes at the opera that season.
words.mnemonic: Picture someone literally coated in banknotes — 'money' plus '-ed' means covered in it.

words.definition: Resembling a grand royal residence; large and magnificent.
words.example: They rented a palatial villa with forty rooms and its own marble ballroom.
words.mnemonic: 'Palatial' hides 'palace' — anything fit for a palace is palatial.

words.definition: Marked by self-indulgent excess or moral decline.
words.example: The party was decadent — champagne fountains, gold-leaf cake, and no thought of the cost.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'decay-dent' — luxury sliding into decay.

words.definition: Devoted to sensual pleasure and comfortable, luxurious living.
words.example: His sybaritic lifestyle revolved around silk sheets, long baths, and endless feasts.
words.mnemonic: From Sybaris, an ancient Greek city whose citizens were famous for pleasure-loving luxury.

words.definition: Devoted to the refined enjoyment of fine food and drink.
words.example: An epicurean at heart, she planned the whole trip around Michelin-starred restaurants.
words.mnemonic: Named after the philosopher Epicurus, long associated with the pursuit of pleasure.

words.definition: Strikingly bold and showy in appearance or behavior.
words.example: In a magenta suit and feathered hat, the flamboyant host commanded every eye in the room.
words.mnemonic: 'Flamboyant' contains 'flame' — bold and flame-like, impossible to ignore.

words.definition: Unpleasantly bright, colorful, or showy in a tasteless way.
words.example: The casino's garish neon signs made her squint and long for a plain white wall.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'glare-ish' — so bright it makes you glare.

words.definition: Excessively showy and bright in a cheap, tasteless manner.
words.example: She wore every ring she owned at once, a gaudy display that clinked with each gesture.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'gawd-y' — so tacky it makes you gasp 'oh gawd.'

words.definition: Covered with elaborate, intricate decoration.
words.example: The ornate ceiling was crowded with gold scrolls, cherubs, and carved vines.
words.mnemonic: 'Ornate' contains 'ornament' — piled high with ornaments.

words.definition: Coated with a thin layer of gold, or superficially rich and glamorous.
words.example: Behind the gilded frames and marble floors, the mansion was quietly drowning in debt.
words.mnemonic: From 'gild,' to coat in gold — a golden surface hiding what lies beneath.

words.definition: Trying to seem more important, cultured, or talented than one really is.
words.example: His pretentious speech was stuffed with French phrases he clearly didn't understand.
words.mnemonic: 'Pretentious' contains 'pretend' — pretending to be grander than you are.

words.definition: Dedicated to the pursuit of pleasure as life's main goal.
words.example: After the windfall, he spent a hedonistic year of parties, yachts, and zero responsibilities.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'hedone,' meaning pleasure — the root of 'hedonism.'

words.definition: A person whose life centers on luxury and bodily pleasures.
words.example: A true voluptuary, he judged each day by its meals, its wines, and its comforts.
words.mnemonic: Linked to 'voluptuous' — someone who chases full, sensual pleasure.

words.definition: Describing rules that limit how much people may spend on luxuries or extravagance.
words.example: Medieval sumptuary rules forbade commoners from wearing the silks and furs reserved for nobility.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'sumptuous' + '-ary' — laws about your sumptuous spending.

words.definition: Having no money, food, or shelter; living in extreme poverty.
words.example: After the flood swept away their home and savings, the family was left completely destitute.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' (away) + 'stitute' (from Latin statuere, to stand) — stripped of everything you stand on.

words.definition: Lacking the money needed for basic comforts and daily survival.
words.example: The clinic offers free care to indigent patients who cannot afford insurance.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'in-dig-ent' — you have to dig through empty pockets and find nothing.

words.definition: Made very poor, or drained of strength and resources.
words.example: Decades of drought left the once-fertile region impoverished and its farmers unable to plant.
words.mnemonic: 'Im-' + 'pover' (poor, like French 'pauvre') — pushed into poorness.

words.definition: A person who has almost no money and depends on charity.
words.example: The prince disguised himself as a pauper, begging coins on the same streets he once ruled.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'pauper' (poor) — the 'pau-' shows up in 'poverty' too.

words.definition: To reduce someone to complete poverty.
words.example: The crushing new taxes threatened to pauperize thousands of small shopkeepers overnight.
words.mnemonic: 'Pauper' + '-ize' — to turn someone into a pauper.

words.definition: A person who lives by asking strangers for money or food.
words.example: A ragged mendicant sat outside the temple, bowl in hand, waiting for travelers to drop a coin.
words.mnemonic: 'Mend-i-can't' — someone who can't mend their fortunes, so they must ask for help.

words.definition: The practice of living by asking others for money or charity.
words.example: Forced out of work, he slipped into mendicancy, holding out a cup at the station each morning.
words.mnemonic: Same 'mend-i-can't' root — the whole way of life of one who can't mend their means.

words.definition: Unable to pay what one owes because debts exceed available money.
words.example: The airline became insolvent when its debts ballooned past anything its ticket sales could cover.
words.mnemonic: 'In-' (not) + 'solvent' (able to dissolve/pay off) — you cannot dissolve your debts.

words.definition: The state of being unable to pay one's debts.
words.example: Mounting losses drove the retailer into insolvency, and administrators soon took over its shops.
words.mnemonic: 'In-' (not) + 'solvency' (ability to pay) — the condition of not being able to pay.

words.definition: Legally declared unable to repay money owed to creditors.
words.example: After the lawsuit wiped out its cash, the studio filed as bankrupt and stopped all production.
words.mnemonic: Italian 'banca rotta' — a broken bench; medieval moneylenders' benches were smashed when they failed.

words.definition: The legal condition of a person or firm unable to repay debts.
words.example: The chain declared bankruptcy, and a judge began dividing its assets among the creditors.
words.mnemonic: 'Banca rotta' (broken bench) + '-cy' — the state of having your money bench smashed.

words.definition: Lacking money and basic necessities; requiring help to get by.
words.example: Volunteers packed boxes of groceries for needy households before the holidays.
words.mnemonic: 'Need' + '-y' — full of need, missing what you need to live.

words.definition: Extremely poor, or so small as to seem contemptible.
words.example: They offered him a beggarly wage that barely covered his bus fare, let alone rent.
words.mnemonic: 'Beggar' + '-ly' — in the manner of a beggar: pitifully meager.

words.definition: Worn so thin that the fabric has become shabby and shows its weave.
words.example: His threadbare coat did nothing to keep out the January wind.
words.mnemonic: thread + bare — rubbed so long that the threads are left bare.

words.definition: Extremely dirty, run-down, and unpleasant, usually because of poverty or neglect.
words.example: The refugees were crammed into a squalid basement with no running water.
words.mnemonic: Picture a squid rotting under a lid — foul, slimy filth.

words.definition: A condition of filth, degradation, and misery caused by poverty or neglect.
words.example: They lived in such squalor that the walls were black with mold.
words.mnemonic: squalor rhymes with 'holler' — you'd holler living in that filth.

words.definition: Involving a bitter struggle to earn a living from poor or barren land.
words.example: She grew up on a hardscrabble farm where every harvest was a gamble.
words.mnemonic: hard + scrabble — you scrabble hard in the dirt for scraps.

words.definition: Restricted by a severe shortage of money.
words.example: After the layoffs, the family had to manage in straitened circumstances.
words.mnemonic: From 'strait,' a narrow passage — your money gets narrow and tight.

words.definition: A very small or inadequate amount of money, especially as pay.
words.example: They paid the seamstresses a pittance for twelve-hour shifts.
words.mnemonic: pity + pence — so few pence it earns nothing but your pity.

words.definition: The condition of surviving on the minimum food and resources needed to stay alive.
words.example: The villagers lived at bare subsistence, growing only enough rice to eat.
words.mnemonic: 'sub' (barely) + 'sist' (to stand) — barely standing, just clinging to life.

words.definition: To keep oneself alive with minimal food or means.
words.example: Stranded on the island, they subsisted on coconuts and rainwater.
words.mnemonic: 'sub' (under, barely) + 'sist' (Latin sistere, to stand) — to barely keep standing.

words.definition: The process of driving people into deep poverty and misery.
words.example: Critics blamed the policy for the immiseration of an entire generation of workers.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'misery' — im-MISERY-ation makes people wretched and poor.

words.definition: The complete collapse of one's wealth, health, or fortunes.
words.example: One reckless investment brought the merchant to total ruin.
words.mnemonic: Picture ancient ruins — crumbled remains of what was once grand and whole.

words.definition: To obtain something through effort, care, or arrangement.
words.example: The quartermaster spent weeks trying to procure enough tents for the entire regiment.
words.mnemonic: PRO + CURE: a pro secures the cure by tracking down and obtaining the medicine.

words.definition: To come to possess or gain something.
words.example: After months of negotiation, the museum was finally able to acquire the ancient bronze statue.
words.mnemonic: A 'quire' is 24 sheets of paper — you get a quire, so ac-QUIRE means to get.

words.definition: Something obtained, or the act of gaining possession of it.
words.example: The tech giant announced its latest acquisition, a small startup with a promising battery design.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a-question' — the buyer asked a question, then closed the purchase.

words.definition: To take something for one's own use, often without permission.
words.example: The general moved to appropriate every truck in the village for the war effort.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'a-PROPER-ty' — you take property and make it your own.

words.definition: To take property from its owner, especially by an authority for public use.
words.example: The new law allowed the state to expropriate farmland to build the highway.
words.mnemonic: EX (out) + PROPER-ty: property is pulled OUT of your hands by the government.

words.definition: To force someone to give up land, property, or a home.
words.example: The flood threatened to dispossess hundreds of families living along the riverbank.
words.mnemonic: DIS (away) + POSSESS: your possessions are stripped away.

words.definition: To steal small items repeatedly in tiny quantities.
words.example: She noticed the intern would pilfer pens and sticky notes from the supply closet each week.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pill + fur' — a sneak pockets a pill and a bit of fur, small stuff at a time.

words.definition: To make full use of something for gain, or to treat someone unfairly for profit.
words.example: The factory owner was accused of trying to exploit workers by paying them far below minimum wage.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'explode' + 'profit' — squeeze it until every last bit of profit bursts out.

words.definition: To waste money, time, or energy little by little on trivial things.
words.example: Don't fritter away your savings on lottery tickets and impulse buys.
words.mnemonic: A fritter is fried batter you nibble bit by bit until it's gone — just like cash slipping away.

words.definition: To reduce spending and use resources carefully.
words.example: With the baby coming, the couple decided to economize by cooking every meal at home.
words.mnemonic: ECONOMY + size it DOWN — shrink your spending.

words.definition: To cut back expenses or scale down operations to save money.
words.example: As sales collapsed, the airline had to retrench, grounding planes and freezing all hiring.
words.mnemonic: RE + TRENCH: dig back into your trench, hunker down, and slash spending to survive.

words.definition: To prevent someone from having or keeping something they need.
words.example: Keeping the lights on all night will deprive you of the deep sleep your body needs.
words.mnemonic: DE (away) + 'prive' (private/have) — take away what someone has.

words.definition: Left without something needed, or desolate from a great loss.
words.example: After the funeral she wandered the empty house, bereft and unable to speak.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'be left' — you are left with nothing.

words.definition: To pay a person in return for work done or services provided.
words.example: The firm promised to remunerate every volunteer generously once the festival turned a profit.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 're-MONEY-rate' — you set a rate of money to hand back for the job.

words.definition: To help pay part of the cost of something so it stays affordable.
words.example: The government chose to subsidize bus fares so poorer commuters could still afford to travel.
words.mnemonic: 'Sub' (under) + 'side' — cash slipped under the table to prop something up.

words.definition: Money given by a government or body to lower the cost of something.
words.example: Without the farming subsidy, many small dairies would have closed within a year.
words.mnemonic: 'Sub' = under — a cushion of cash set under a struggling business to keep it upright.

words.definition: Relating to or consisting of money.
words.example: She had no pecuniary motive; she tutored the children purely for the joy of it.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'pecunia' (money) came from 'pecus' (cattle), once real wealth — picture a 'peculiar' rich cow.

words.definition: Relating to government revenue, taxes, and public spending.
words.example: The new chancellor tightened fiscal policy, raising taxes to shrink the deficit.
words.mnemonic: 'Fisc' was the ancient Roman state treasury basket — fiscal is anything in that money basket.

words.definition: Relating to currency or the supply of it within an economy.
words.example: The central bank's monetary decisions pushed interest rates higher overnight.
words.mnemonic: 'Moneta' was the Roman temple where coins were struck — the root of both 'money' and 'mint'.

words.definition: Producing a great deal of profit or wealth.
words.example: Her side business selling handmade candles proved surprisingly lucrative.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'LOOT-crative' — an activity that creates loot.

words.definition: Bringing a good financial return; well paid.
words.example: He left teaching for a more remunerative career in software consulting.
words.mnemonic: Hear 're-MONEY-rative' — work that keeps paying good money back to you.

words.definition: Relating to trade and the business of buying and selling goods.
words.example: The old port city grew rich on its mercantile links across the Mediterranean.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'mercari' (to trade) — the same root that gives us 'market' and 'commerce'.

words.definition: Seeking to exploit or harm others for one's own gain.
words.example: Predatory lenders trapped borrowers with hidden fees and crushing interest.
words.mnemonic: Think 'predator' — a hunting beast circling weaker prey, waiting to pounce.

words.definition: Charging unfairly high interest on a loan.
words.example: The pawnbroker's usurious rates left the family deeper in debt each month.
words.mnemonic: 'You-SURE-ee-us?' — 'You sure he's charging THAT much interest?!'

words.definition: Payment or profit received from holding an office or job.
words.example: As a trustee she accepted no emolument, serving the charity entirely for free.
words.mnemonic: 'E-moll-ument' — picture the 'moolah' you collect just for holding a post.

words.definition: A fixed, regular sum paid as an allowance, often to students or clergy.
words.example: The fellowship came with a modest monthly stipend to cover his living costs.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'stips' (small coin) + 'pendere' (to weigh out) — a weighed-out little payment.

words.definition: A share of profits paid regularly to a company's shareholders.
words.example: After a strong year, the board raised the dividend, delighting investors.
words.mnemonic: 'Divide-end' — profit is divided up and the end slice goes out to the owners.

words.definition: The total income a business or government takes in.
words.example: Streaming subscriptions now generate more revenue than the studio's box-office sales.
words.mnemonic: From French 'revenir' (to come back) — the money that comes back in to the business.

words.definition: To penalize someone by taking money, or to cheat a person out of funds through deception.
words.example: The crooked inspector would mulct small shop owners, pocketing fines he invented on the spot.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like "milk" — a swindler will milk, or mulct, victims of their cash.

description: mid-frequency and academic register — wealth and poverty
